newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. stand on reactors attracts flak in India.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stand on reactors attracts flak in India.

text.p: Indian analysts on Saturday slammed the United States for urging Russia to drop a planned sale of two light-water nuclear reactors to India, saying Washington was adopting a double standard.

"In reality Americans are already endorsing the supply of certain reactors to North Korea," C. Uday Bhaskar, deputy director of the state-funded Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (IDSA), told Reuters.
Bhaskar said: "It had been agreed that U.S. would supply two light water reactors of 1,000 megawatts each to North Korea as per an agreement signed in June 1995."

The New York Times reported on Thursday that United States has urged Russia to drop its planned sale of two light water nuclear reactors to India, which is not a signatory of the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
The newspaper quoted an unidentified senior U.S. official saying the sale would be a setback to global efforts to stop the spread of nuclear weapons.

The reactors being negotiated with Russia are to be installed in southern India and can produce one million kilowatts of power each. India says it needs nuclear plants because of a massive electricity shortage.
Washington has said that Russia, as a signatory to a 1992 suppliers' agreement, should not be selling such nuclear technologies to would-be nuclear powers such as India.

The suppliers' agreement forbids suppliers from exporting nuclear technology to aspiring nuclear powers. Sales are forbidden to countries not formally recognised as nuclear weapons states and which do not allow international inspections of key nuclear institutes, a key provision of the NPT.
Only the United States, Russia, Britain, France and China are recognised as nuclear weapon states.
India detonated a nuclear device in 1974 but says it has not built a nuclear bomb.

Last year, India opposed a global nuclear test ban treaty saying it would not lead to elimination of nuclear weapons as it allowed the five acknowledged nuclear weapons powers to continue developing and improving the quality of their atomic arms.
Indian commentators said Washington was inconsistent in urging Russia to stop the sale of light water reactors.
"This is an old issue. Nobody is worried about the U.S. statement. There was no new provocation for this," said K.S. Jayaraman, the science editor of Press Trust of India (PTI).
"This is another example of how U.S. is inconsistent in its dealing as far as nuclear negotiations were concerned," Bhaskar said, adding sales of nuclear power reactors have become bilateral issues.
"Chinese have gone ahead and supplied power reactors to Pakistan," he said.
India and the former Soviet Union began talks on the supply of the two reactors in 1987.
